strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: common visual brain decoding metrics can report near-saturated scores despite obvious semantic reconstruction failures.

SEED is simple, interpretable, and practically useful: Object F1, caption similarity, and EffNet each capture different semantic aspects, and the examples make the failure modes of individual components easy to understand.
The paper provides a human-judgment meta-evaluation with multiple correlation measures, and SEED substantially improves over the evaluated alternatives on this set.
The semantic near-miss analysis is a nice diagnostic contribution that highlights a concrete failure mode of current decoding models beyond aggregate scores.
The proposed pairwise hinge loss is easy to integrate with embedding-based decoding models and is tested across several representative baselines.
weaknesses: The novelty of the main metric is limited: SEED is a plain average of off-the-shelf detector, captioner, sentence encoder, and EfficientNet scores. The paper does not provide a principled formulation or strong justification for equal weighting beyond empirical performance on the same human-rating set.

The human evaluation is too narrow to fully support the central claim. Ratings are collected only for 1,000 MindEye2 reconstructions from NSD/COCO, so it is unclear whether the metric generalizes to other reconstruction models, datasets, stimulus distributions, or failure modes.

There appears to be no held-out validation for metric design. The same human judgments seem to motivate component choice, compare alternatives, and report final performance, which risks overfitting the metric to this specific annotation set.

Important human-study details are missing or underdeveloped, including inter-annotator agreement, worker filtering beyond broad MTurk requirements, treatment of student versus MTurk annotators, statistical confidence intervals, significance tests, and whether the low payment affected annotation quality.

SEED inherits brittleness from its external models. Object F1 is restricted to 82 object categories and ignores count/location unless ablated in a very limited way; caption similarity can miss visual differences or overemphasize text templates; EffNet can be class-biased. These limitations matter for brain decoding but are not deeply addressed.

The pairwise hinge loss results are not very convincing. Improvements in Table 3 are small, some baseline metrics degrade, no variance or statistical testing is reported, and qualitative examples are selected for cases where SEED benefits most.

The reproduced training setup modifies at least MindEye2 substantially due to compute limits, making it hard to assess whether the loss improves strong published systems under their original settings.

The claims that SEED should serve as a go-to metric and that the loss consistently enhances semantic decoding are stronger than the evidence currently supports. More cross-model, cross-dataset, held-out human validation would be needed for a top-tier acceptance-level contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem in visual brain decoding: existing metrics can give high scores to reconstructions that humans would judge as semantically wrong.

The human-rating study is a useful direction, and the paper compares several existing metrics against human semantic similarity judgments using pairwise accuracy, Kendall's tau-b, and Pearson correlation.

The proposed SEED metric is simple and interpretable: combining object detection, caption similarity, and EffNet features makes the evaluation easier to reason about than opaque two-way identification scores.
The paper includes some helpful qualitative analyses of failure cases, including semantic near-misses where reconstructions preserve a broad category but miss the specific object.
The authors attempt to go beyond evaluation by adding a pairwise hinge loss and testing it across multiple visual decoding models.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not very novel. SEED is a simple average of object-category F1, caption-embedding similarity, and an existing EffNet metric. This is a plausible engineering metric, but the paper does not provide a sufficiently deep methodological advance for a top-tier AI venue.

The meta-evaluation is narrow and risks overfitting. The human ratings are collected only for 1,000 MindEye2 reconstruction pairs from NSD, and SEED's components are selected and validated on essentially the same setting. It is unclear whether the metric generalizes to other decoding models, datasets, image domains, reconstruction qualities, or human populations.

The human study is underdescribed and potentially weak. The paper reports 22 ratings per pair, but gives little analysis of inter-annotator agreement, rater quality control, demographic/task effects, confidence intervals, or statistical significance of differences between metrics.

The improvement of SEED over EffNet is modest relative to the simplicity of the combination. EffNet alone is already strong, and the paper does not convincingly show that the added complexity of object detection and captioning yields robust gains outside the development set.

The metric has substantial dependency issues. Object F1 is limited to 82 COCO-style categories and ignores counts by default; Cap-Sim depends on captioner and sentence-embedding errors; EffNet can be class-biased. These known failure modes are acknowledged through examples but not systematically resolved.

The pairwise hinge loss contribution is weakly supported. Quantitative gains in Table 3 are very small and mixed across metrics, with some metrics worsening. The claim that the loss significantly enhances semantic decoding is not justified without statistical testing, stronger baselines, and clearer evaluation of practical significance.

The reproduced training setup changes important baseline details, including reducing the MindEye2 latent dimension and removing the low-level pipeline due to compute constraints. This makes the loss-function comparisons less conclusive and harder to interpret as improvements over the actual methods.

The paper's claims are stronger than its evidence. It presents SEED as a go-to framework and claims comprehensive evaluation, but the evidence is mostly one dataset, one main human-rating source, and a metric-selection procedure that appears tuned to that source.

Ethical and societal issues are barely discussed despite the brain-decoding context. A paper on evaluating reconstruction of perceived images should address privacy, consent, misuse, and limits of interpretation more carefully.

Overall, the paper identifies a real weakness in the field's evaluation practice, but the proposed solution and evidence are not sufficiently novel, rigorous, or general to meet the acceptance bar for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: current visual brain decoding metrics can look saturated while reconstructions still miss semantically important content.
The proposed SEED metric is simple, interpretable, and well motivated, combining complementary signals from object presence, caption similarity, and EfficientNet features.
The paper collects human judgments for 1,000 GT/reconstruction pairs with 22 ratings each, and uses multiple meta-evaluation criteria: pairwise accuracy, Kendall's tau-b, and Pearson correlation.

Empirical results show a clear improvement in alignment with human judgments over commonly used metrics, with SEED outperforming strong alternatives such as CLIP, SwAV, EffNet alone, and caption/VQA-based variants.
The analysis of component failure cases and the semantic near-miss phenomenon is insightful and helps explain why existing metrics can obscure meaningful reconstruction errors.
The proposed pairwise hinge loss is easy to integrate into existing CLIP-embedding-based decoding models and is evaluated across several representative baselines.
weaknesses: The central meta-evaluation appears to use the same human judgment set both to motivate/select the SEED components and to report final alignment, with no held-out validation or cross-validation; this raises a real risk of overfitting or data-driven metric selection.

Human evaluation is limited to MindEye2 reconstructions on NSD/COCO images, so it is unclear whether SEED's superiority generalizes to other reconstruction models, datasets, image domains, or substantially different failure modes.

The human study details are underdeveloped: inter-annotator agreement, attention checks, rater calibration, treatment of student vs MTurk annotators, and compensation/quality considerations are not sufficiently analyzed.

SEED is an unweighted average of three metrics with different ranges and statistical properties; the paper does not deeply justify calibration, normalization, or whether the averaging rule is robust beyond this dataset.

Object F1 is more restricted than the presentation suggests: despite using a grounding model, the evaluation is based on a fixed 82-category COCO-style vocabulary and ignores counts, relationships, and many non-object semantic attributes.

The pairwise hinge loss results are relatively modest, especially for MindEye2, and the paper claims significant or consistent semantic improvement without statistical tests, variance across seeds, or clear evidence that improvements are practically large.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: the paper promises release of human judgments, but code, exact generated captions/detections, metric preprocessing, and model reproduction details would need to be available for the contribution to be fully usable.
The paper's strongest contribution is evaluation rather than a new decoding method; the added training loss is useful but not as convincingly established as the metric contribution.

strengths: The paper targets a real and timely evaluation problem in visual brain decoding: standard two-way identification metrics can saturate and can be poorly aligned with semantic human judgments.
The proposed SEED metric is simple, interpretable, and practically usable, combining object-level matching, caption-level semantic similarity, and EfficientNet feature similarity.
The human evaluation on 1,000 NSD/MindEye2 reconstruction pairs with 22 raters is a meaningful contribution, and the reported inter-rater agreement is strong.

The meta-evaluation is reasonably broad over commonly used decoding metrics and shows consistent improvements for SEED over existing metrics, including statistically significant gains over EffNet on the main dataset.
The paper includes useful diagnostic analyses and shows how the metric can reveal failure modes such as semantic near-misses and missing semantic details across several recent decoding models.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: SEED is a simple average of three off-the-shelf components, two of which are straightforward applications of object detection and image captioning/text embedding. The paper's main value is empirical rather than algorithmic.

The main metric design and evaluation appear to use the same human-rated NSD/MindEye2 data, raising concern about selection bias or overfitting when choosing components and combinations. There is no clear held-out validation/test split for metric development versus final meta-evaluation.

The external robustness check is small: only 50 GOD/Mind-Vis examples rated by 10 student volunteers. This is helpful but not enough to establish broad generalization across datasets, subjects, stimulus distributions, and decoder families.

Important modern perceptual/semantic image similarity baselines are missing or underexplored, such as DINO/DINOv2 features, LPIPS, DreamSim, ImageReward-like or VLM/LLM-based pairwise judges, and stronger CLIP variants. This weakens the claim that SEED is the best available semantic metric.

The human evaluation protocol lacks detail on quality control, rater demographics, exact instructions, treatment of ties, calibration, and aggregation. The MTurk payment of $0.03 per pair also raises concerns about annotation quality and fairness, even though agreement is reported.

Object F1 depends on a fixed 82-category vocabulary and ignores object count, spatial relations, attributes, and fine-grained categories; these limitations are acknowledged partly, but they can be central for semantic fidelity in natural scenes.
Cap-Sim inherits captioning model biases and may miss visually important details not verbalized by the captioner. The paper does not deeply analyze how caption errors propagate into the final metric.

The statistical testing bootstraps only over evaluators, but uncertainty also arises over image pairs, model choices, and dataset/model selection. More complete confidence intervals or paired tests over examples would make the evidence stronger.

The paper sometimes overstates the neuroscience motivation: the connection to two-stage visual attention is intuitive but not technically necessary for the metric and does not strongly constrain the design.

Reproducibility is partially addressed, but the manuscript text shows an incomplete code/data availability line, and exact implementation details for normalization before averaging SEED components are not fully clear.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important issue in visual brain decoding: commonly used two-way identification metrics can saturate and may fail to reflect semantic errors in reconstructions.

The proposed metric is interpretable: Object F1, caption similarity, and EffNet each correspond to understandable aspects of semantic similarity, and the qualitative examples help illustrate what the metric is capturing.
The authors collect human similarity judgments and report inter-rater agreement, which is a useful contribution for studying evaluation metrics in this domain.
The paper includes some helpful analysis of failure modes in current decoding models, such as semantic near-misses and cases where objects are recovered but attributes/background details are missed.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is limited: SEED is a simple average of an object detector score, caption embedding similarity, and an existing EfficientNet feature correlation. This is plausible but not technically deep or clearly novel enough for a top-tier AI venue.

The main meta-evaluation appears vulnerable to metric selection on the same human-evaluation set used for reporting performance. The appendix shows that combinations were explored using these correlations, but there is no clear held-out validation split to demonstrate that SEED was not tuned to this dataset.

The improvement over EffNet, the strongest existing baseline, is modest in the main setting, and the statistical test bootstraps over evaluators rather than addressing image-level variation, model-level variation, or multiple metric-combination comparisons.

The generalization evidence is weak. The secondary GOD/Mind-Vis study has only 50 examples and 10 student raters, which is too small to support broad claims of robustness across datasets and decoding models.
The evaluation is narrow: the human ratings are primarily collected on MindEye2 reconstructions from NSD, so conclusions about visual brain decoding models in general are under-supported.

The paper overstates novelty in places, especially around caption-based image similarity, which is closely related to existing captioning/VQA/text-based evaluation approaches in image generation and retrieval.

Object F1 has conceptual weaknesses that are not fully resolved: it ignores counts, spatial relations, object hierarchy, and categories outside a fixed list; it also depends on detector confidence calibration, which may differ between natural images and distorted reconstructions.
The robustness experiments over off-the-shelf components are summarized only coarsely and do not sufficiently analyze when detector/captioner failures drive SEED errors.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript text: the claimed code/data link appears missing, and important details about annotation instructions, quality control, demographics, and aggregation are limited.
Several claims, such as SEED being a more reliable standard or providing general guidance for future decoding models, are stronger than what the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap in visual brain decoding: existing identification-style metrics can look saturated while reconstructions still contain obvious semantic errors. The motivation is compelling and well illustrated.

SEED is simple, interpretable, and practically useful: combining object-level matching, caption-level similarity, and EffNet features gives a metric that can expose different failure modes rather than only producing a scalar score.

The human evaluation effort is a real strength. The main NSD/MindEye2 study uses 1,000 image pairs with 22 ratings per pair and reports high inter-rater agreement, providing meaningful evidence that SEED better aligns with human semantic judgments than common metrics.

The empirical results are convincing enough for a marginal accept: SEED improves over strong existing metrics such as EffNet across pairwise accuracy, Kendall correlation, and Pearson correlation, and the authors include bootstrap confidence intervals for the key SEED-vs-EffNet comparison.
The paper goes beyond metric proposal by using SEED to analyze recent decoding models and identify concrete failure modes such as semantic near-misses and missing fine-grained semantic details.

The appendix includes useful ablations and robustness checks, including alternative detector/caption/text-embedding choices, component combinations, VLM-derived object categories, and qualitative worst-case analyses.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate. SEED is a straightforward average of three off-the-shelf signals, and the main contribution is primarily empirical/meta-evaluative rather than a technically deep new metric.

The metric design appears partially selected on the same human evaluation data used to validate it. The paper motivates components post hoc and reports all combinations, but it does not clearly separate metric development, validation, and final testing. This raises some risk of overfitting to the main NSD/MindEye2 human dataset.

Generalization evidence is limited. The secondary robustness study uses only 50 image pairs and 10 student raters on GOD/Mind-Vis, which is helpful but too small to fully support broad claims that SEED generalizes across datasets, models, and decoding regimes.

SEED inherits systematic biases and blind spots from off-the-shelf object detectors, captioners, sentence encoders, and ImageNet-trained features. The paper acknowledges this, but the resulting metric may under-evaluate malformed or unusual reconstructions and images containing objects outside the fixed category set.

Object F1 discards count, location, and fine-grained object relationships; the appendix finds these additions do not help on the tested data, but the limitation remains important for semantic fidelity in richer scenes.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially that the metric is inspired by human visual attention. The neuroscience framing is plausible but fairly loose; the metric is not really validated as a model of human visual processing, only as a correlate of human similarity ratings.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript text: the abstract and reproducibility statement say code/data are available, but the URL appears missing in the provided PDF. Details such as exact prompts, preprocessing, normalization, and model versions/checkpoints should be made fully explicit.

The paper would be stronger with comparisons to additional modern image similarity or multimodal evaluation metrics beyond the commonly used brain-decoding metrics and a small set of VQA-score alternatives. Caption-based and VLM-based evaluation is a broad area, so positioning and baselines could be more comprehensive.
